title: Ordering at a Café
description: Order a karak, a plate of something, ask for it without onion and with extra sauce, say it's delicious or too spicy, and call for the bill — plus the polite fight over who pays it.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — transactional script with a grammar hook. Café scenes supply the orders; the imperative-plus-suffix pattern (bring me, give us) is lifted out and drilled, then the learner places a full order aloud.
unlock_condition: ≥12/16 on the menu-and-order listening quiz and a complete recorded order with one modification
can_do: Say something is delicious, spicy or sweet

grammar.title: Bring me, give us: a command with the person stuck on the end
grammar.explanation: Orders are commands with 'me' or 'us' attached. The command comes first — جيب 'bring', عطـ 'give', حط 'put' — then the person: جيب لي 'bring me', عطني 'give me', عطنا 'give us', حط لي 'put for me'. Notice the two shapes: جيب and حط take لي / لنا as a separate little word (جيب لي، حط لنا), while عطـ takes the ending straight on (عطني، عطنا). To a woman the command itself changes: جيبي لي، عطيني; to more than one person, جيبوا لنا، عطونا. Add لو سمحت at the end and the order is polite. Never the formal أحضر لي or هات (which is Egyptian).

culture.title: Who pays, how sweet, and the tip
culture.note: When the bill comes there will be a fight — a real one, with hands reaching and voices rising — over who pays. The one who invited (عزم) pays, and everyone else must try at least once; الحساب علي 'the bill's on me' is the opening move, and لا والله، خلها علي the counter-move. Do not just let a Gulf host pay silently; the attempt is the courtesy. Tea and coffee are ordered with their sugar level: سكر زيادة, سكر عادي, سكر خفيف or بدون سكر; the milky spiced كرك is the Gulf café drink and comes sweet unless you say otherwise. Tipping is light — rounding up or a few riyals — and never expected at a street stall.

phrases.english: No, really, leave it to me

vocabulary.teaching_note: Emphatic ط. The noun طلب is 'an order' — طلبك جاهز 'your order is ready' is what you hear at the counter. 'To order delivery' is أطلب دليفري.
vocabulary.image_scene: A customer at a counter pointing at a menu board, the cashier taking a note.

example.english: What do you want to order?

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone ordering at a counter or table; طلب / أطلب said as they choose.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The order phrase: جيب 'bring' + لي 'for me'. Kuwaitis and Emiratis say the ج as y: yiib li. Written as one word (جيبلي) as often as two. Never هات, which is Egyptian.
vocabulary.image_scene: A seated customer raising a hand slightly toward a waiter carrying a tray.
vocabulary.video_hint: An order being placed — جيب لي / جيبلي — with the item named.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Always with the ال. The single word, said to the waiter with a small writing gesture, is enough: الحساب لو سمحت. The bank word 'account' is the same, so context does the work.
vocabulary.image_scene: A small folder with a receipt and a pen being placed on a café table.
vocabulary.video_hint: The bill being asked for or fought over at the end of a restaurant scene.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Two dh sounds, long ii between them. The praise a cook wants to hear; in casual talk حلو covers it too, but لذيذ is specifically about taste. Feminine لذيذة.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person tasting a spoonful with closed eyes and a delighted face.
vocabulary.video_hint: A food reviewer's first bite — لذيذ! — with the dish on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Doubled r, ق as g. Gulf speakers also just say حار — the same word as 'hot' from Stage 1 — so if someone asks حار؟ about food they mean spicy. Chili itself is شطة or فلفل.
vocabulary.image_scene: A red chili on a plate with a small flame icon, a diner fanning their mouth.

example.english: The food is a bit spicy

vocabulary.video_hint: A spicy-food challenge or a diner warning حار / حراق.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sweet, and by extension 'nice, lovely' — a beautiful place is حلو too. For tea, حلو means too much sugar. Feminine حلوة (ḥilwa); sweets are حلويات.
vocabulary.image_scene: A plate of syrupy luqaimat dumplings drizzled with date syrup.
vocabulary.video_hint: Dessert or sweet tea on screen with حلو said about the taste.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The modifier word every order needs: بدون بصل 'no onion', بدون سكر 'no sugar'. Long uu. Older speakers say بلا for the same thing.
vocabulary.image_scene: A burger with an onion ring crossed out beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: A customer customising an order — بدون … — at a counter.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The pair of بدون: شاي مع نعناع 'tea with mint'. You already know it with a person on the end (معي 'with me'); here it stands alone before a thing. Ends in ع — do not swallow it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A glass of tea with a sprig of fresh mint in it on a tray.
vocabulary.video_hint: An order specifying an extra — مع حليب / مع نعناع — at a café.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The English word, and what everyone says; قائمة is on the printed cover only. Kuwaitis also say لستة (from 'list'). Ask for it with عطني المنيو or جيب لي المنيو.
vocabulary.image_scene: A café menu board with Arabic and English items and prices.

example.english: Could I have the menu, please?

vocabulary.video_hint: A menu handed over or read aloud in a restaurant review.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Another English loan. But you rarely address a waiter as ويتر: you catch his eye with لو سمحت, يا أخوي or — in Saudi cafés — يا كابتن. The Egyptian جرسون is understood but sounds foreign.
vocabulary.image_scene: A waiter in a black apron carrying a tray of tea glasses between tables.

example.english: The waiter brought us the tea quickly

vocabulary.video_hint: A waiter at the table in a restaurant scene; the customer calling لو سمحت / كابتن.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A mug or paper cup: كوب كرك. The tiny handleless Arabic-coffee cup is a فنجان and a tea glass is a كاسة — three words for three drinks. The Egyptian كوباية is not Gulf.
vocabulary.image_scene: A paper takeaway cup of milky tea with a lid, steam rising.

example.english: Two cups of karak, one without sugar

vocabulary.video_hint: Cups being handed through a karak stall window; كوب or كاسة said.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Two syllables in Gulf: ṣa-ḥan. Also a portion: صحن مندي 'a plate of mandi' is how you order. Plural صحون. Emphatic ص then a throaty ح.
vocabulary.image_scene: A round plate heaped with rice and grilled chicken on a restaurant table.

example.english: A plate of chicken mandi, please

vocabulary.video_hint: A plate set down in a food vlog; صحن in the order.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'I have become full' — a past-tense verb, which is why it ends in -t. The only acceptable way to stop a host from serving more: والله شبعت. Feminine and masculine are the same.
vocabulary.image_scene: A diner leaning back with a hand on their stomach, an empty plate in front.

example.english: That's it, I'm full, thank you

vocabulary.video_hint: The end of a meal — شبعت — often while food is still being pushed across.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Emphatic ط then ع back to back — a hard pair; go slowly: maṭ-ʿam. The café is كافيه or كوفي; a street stall is بسطة. Plural مطاعم.
vocabulary.image_scene: A restaurant frontage at night with a lit sign, families entering.

example.english: This is the best restaurant in the neighbourhood

vocabulary.video_hint: A food-review channel arriving at a restaurant; مطعم in the intro.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Gulf's café drink — strong tea boiled with milk, sugar and cardamom, sold from roadside windows for a couple of riyals. Ordering one by name is the fastest way to sound at home.
vocabulary.image_scene: A small paper cup of orange-brown milky tea at a roadside stall window.

example.english: Shall we go and have a karak?

vocabulary.video_hint: A karak stall in a vlog; the order shouted through the window.

vocabulary.teaching_note: From سفر 'travel' — food that travels. The counter question everywhere: سفري ولا هنا؟ 'takeaway or here?'. The English تيك أواي is heard too.
vocabulary.image_scene: A cashier holding up a paper bag with a question mark, a table behind.
vocabulary.video_hint: The counter question سفري ولا هنا؟ in a café scene.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Hi, what would you like to order?

dialogue.speaker: Saud
dialogue.arabic: جيب لنا صحن مندي دجاج وكوبين كرك
dialogue.transliteration: jiib lana ṣaḥan mandi dijaaj w-kuubayn karak

sound_spotlight.example: جيب لي (jiib li)، حط لنا (ḥuṭṭ lana)
sound_spotlight.explanation: 'For me' and 'for us' are said as a tiny unstressed word right after the command: jiib-li, ḥuṭṭ-lana. Captions write them apart or together (جيبلي); your ear will hear one word.
Two deep sounds back to back — an emphatic t followed by the throat squeeze of ع. Say maṭ, stop, then ʿam; speed comes later.
Saudis say jiib; Kuwaitis, Emiratis, Qataris and Bahrainis say yiib. Same word, and the café will understand either.

lesson_sequence.detail: A 45-second clip of an order at a Gulf café, no captions: the learner watches the menu, the pointing, the tray arriving.
Sixteen cards with illustration and audio; food adjectives play in a reaction (لذيذ! حراق!) and the command phrases inside a full order.
Grammar card: جيب لي / عطني / حط لي with the person swapping (me, us, f, pl); then a tap-to-build exercise assembling orders from command + item + modifier.
Listening quiz: eight spoken orders; the learner ticks the items and modifiers (مع / بدون) on a menu card.
Role-play: the app is the waiter; the learner orders a drink with a sugar level, a plate with one change, and asks for the bill. Then the bill fight: the learner must say الحساب علي once.
Score screen; the learner's order plays back beside a native one. Nudge: next café visit, order in Gulf.

real_world_prompts.prompt: At your next café, order in Gulf even if the barista replies in English: جيب لي كرك بدون سكر، سفري.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. A low-stakes real transaction using the command + suffix pattern.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you eat with Arabic speakers, try الحساب علي when the bill arrives — and enjoy the argument.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day nudge. The culture note turned into an action.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Watch a Gulf food review and note every adjective: لذيذ، حلو، حراق. Which does the reviewer use most?
real_world_prompts.context: Homework card. Passive recognition of the three taste words in authentic speech.

video_needs.scene: Ordering at a café or restaurant: the menu, the waiter, modifications (بدون / مع), the reaction to the first bite, and the bill at the end.
